title: Freddy vs. Jason
full_review:
Just when you thought it had dredged the dregs of the summer movie barrel, Hollywood serves up a double helping of gore in the abysmally dreadful slasherfest "Freddy vs. Jason" (New Line).

Hoping to make a killing at the box office by cross-pollinating two of the most successful horror franchises, director Ronny Yu delivers, in a flick boasting Freddy and Jason, the biggest "hack job."

At the risk of dignifying this execrable exercise in bloody excess, the plot -- or what passes as one -- goes something like this: Freddy Krueger (Robert Englund), the sadistic sandman of "A Nightmare on Elm Street" infamy, is trapped in hell.

After seven increasingly ridiculous films, the parents of Springwood have wised up and taken pharmaceutical measures to prevent the town's teen-age residents from dreaming, effectively denying Freddy entree into their nocturnal noggins and systemically erasing the collective memory of his heinous crimes.

Having been rendered impotent, Freddy is left with little to do with his satanic sabbatical but plot revenge, which, in one of the film's many ludicrous conceits, involves enlisting the service of Jason Voorhees (Ken Kirzinger), the hockey-masked killing machine of "Friday the 13th" renown. Freddy, disguised as Jason's domineering mother, convinces him to take his own brand of misanthropic mischief to Elm Street in order to raise some hell -- literally -- thus paving the way for the dream demon's return.

The remainder of the derivative drivel -- which steals unapologetically from the "Big Book of Slasher Cliches" -- is nothing more than a formulaic series of graphic slayings, as Freddy and Jason go on a killing spree, engaging in a grisly game of one-upmanship, mowing down Springwood's preternaturally good-looking, oversexed teen populace.

Of course, Jason has too much fun to just bow out quietly once he has raised the townspeople's fear factor sufficiently enough to trigger nightmares -- releasing Freddy from his purgatorial imprisonment and leading to an all-out, no-holds-barred showdown between the two homicidal heavyweights.

The film's pairing of screen villains is not new to the horror genre, which has boasted twin bills ranging from the entertainingly atmospheric "Frankenstein Meets the Wolf Man" (1943) to such late-night fodder as "Dracula vs. Frankenstein" (1971) and "King Kong vs. Godzilla" (1962). But unlike these midnight movies, "Freddy vs. Jason" is something much darker than studio execs hoping to capitalize on offering two maniacs for the price of one.

The film is driven by a repulsive impulse to treat graphic violence as entertainment. Classic horror movies portrayed their respective fiends as misunderstood outcasts. More often than not it was they who were destroyed by cruel intolerance, thus gaining viewers' sympathy. But in films such as this one, serial killers are treated like rock stars, cheered on by enthusiastic fans every time they rack up another notch on their machete, earning bonus points if the method of slaughter employed is exceptionally gruesome.

Part and parcel with this coarsening is the film's promotion of substance abuse and casual sex -- both staples of the slasher milieu. However in a genre that prides itself on its lowest-common-denominator mentality, "Freddy vs. Jason" lowers the bar by including a scene in which a local slacker violates a drunken girl passed out in a cornfield.

The film also endorses a disheartening suspicion of and antagonism toward authority figures, especially parents, a thematic bedrock of horror flicks dating back to the 1950s.

The film ends with a wink -- literally -- strongly hinting that, like their implacable protagonists, these franchises just won't die; that's bad news except for those who own stock in the company that manufactures fake blood. Several of Freddy's victims plead to be awakened from their nightmares -- an unlikely request from anyone lucky enough to doze off during this bad dream.

Due to pervasive graphic violence, teen sexual encounters with nudity, recurring drug abuse, as well as much rough language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
